Intuitive

in-TOO-ih-tiv — something intuitive just feels right without needing to be explained. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Intuitive is known or perceived by intuition; easily and instinctively understood.

The new remote control was so intuitive that even her grandmother figured it out without reading the manual.

Worked Example

A toddler picks up a tablet for the very first time and, without anyone showing her how, immediately starts swiping and tapping to open a game, exactly as the designers hoped she would.

Understanding how to use something instantly, without needing instructions, is exactly what intuitive means. Unlike 'simple,' which just means easy, intuitive specifically means it feels natural right away.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

instinctive: based on instinct rather than conscious thought

natural: coming easily, without needing to be taught

user-friendly: easy for people to understand and use

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

confusing: difficult to understand

complicated: involving many confusing parts

Where it sits · how automatically it comes to you — easy → intuitive → instinctive

easy vs. intuitive: Easy is weaker and more general than intuitive — something easy just doesn't take much effort, while intuitive means it feels natural and obvious without ever being taught.

instinctive vs. intuitive: Instinctive can feel even more automatic than intuitive: intuitive describes something that's easy to grasp with a little thought, but instinctive suggests no thought is needed at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: upon, into (Latin)

Root — tuit

Root — tuit: to look, to gaze; to watch over (from Latin tueri, 'to look at, to watch')

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: tending to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: In- ('upon, into') + tuit ('to look, to gaze' — from Latin tueri) + -ive ('tending to'): Latin intueri meant 'to look upon, to consider.' Something intuitive, at its root, is understood just by 'looking upon' it, with no need for a deeper explanation.

Use the root in a new word: tuition

Use the root in a new word: tuition: Her parents saved for years to cover the cost of her college tuition.
